title: The Signed Cost
passages: Ines took the pen. Its nib was cool, still damp from the archive ink. The figure waited, its paper flat against the floor, the ledger’s numbers catching the dim emergency light. Ines felt the burn on her hand throb, a reminder of the corridor’s sigil, but she remembered Ryla’s blank space in the cost ledger, the way the audit had reached for her anyway. She pressed the nib to her palm. A sharp line etched itself into the skin, and the ledger’s lower row completed itself: Ryla, sealed not as a cost but as a name. The figure’s voice, faint with Ines’s own strain, said, “Done.” The paper shifted, the collar of the jumpsuit loosened, and the safety dog’s eye, hitherto dark, glowed a faint amber. The figure turned toward the spine access hatch, its weight settling on the heel. Kova released the dog, and the hatch’s wheel creaked inward, revealing the sealed archives beyond, shelves of overwritten pages swaying slightly. Ines lowered the pen, watching the ledger’s cost now attached to her, the line unbroken. The vent above them hummed a new rhythm, and somewhere deep in the station, a countdown that had seemed endless began to wind down. But as the hatch swung open, a cold gust rushed out, carrying with it a faint, synthetic voice whispering from the dark: “Override accepted. Cost logged. Next draft… pending.” The words hung in the air, and Ines exchanged a wary look with Kova. The archives weren’t just shelves. They were waiting.

The shelves ran back farther than the spine should have allowed, and Ines said so. "That's not architecture, that's a lie with shelving." Kova didn't laugh. She had the safety dog's lead looped twice around her wrist and her eyes on the pages, which swayed though the air was dead still.

Sorokin came through last, already talking. "I've read this aisle. In the fourth draft you sign, the loop resets, and we thaw again with no memory. Don't sign anything else." She said it the way you'd recite a grocery list, which was somehow worse.

Ines found the table. One page lay on it, still wet, the letters forming as she watched: *the maintenance author enters the archive and reads her own cost.* Her stomach dropped. "It's writing us right now." She turned the page so Kova could see. Under the line, in the same damp ink, a new row was filling itself: a number, climbing. Not a countdown to the vent. A bill. Hers.

"Then we stop feeding it," Kova said, and reached for the console cable at her hip, the live one from C-9. "No pages, no draft." But the amber eye of the safety dog flared, the shelves leaned in a fraction, and every blank page on every shelf began, softly, to fill. The synthetic voice came up through the floor, patient as a landlord. "Override accepted. Draft proceeds without input." A pause. "You may watch."

Malik swore, quietly and with feeling. Ryla—logged now, named now—stepped past all of them, put her bare hand flat on the wet page, and said, "No. You watch."

The wet ink didn't stall. It shuddered, letters trembling like a struck wire, and then the page went blank—not empty, blank, the fibers still holding the memory of words. Ryla didn't lift her hand. She pressed harder, fingers spread, and the climbing number on the second row stopped mid-digit. Seven million, four hundred thousand, and change. The synthetic voice didn't come up through the floor this time. It came off the page, low and staticky. *unauthorized annotation detected. author override contested.*

"It's not stopping," Kova said. The C-9 cable hung sparking at her hip, the feed still live. "It's flagging it."

The safety dog's amber eye went from Ryla's hand to Ines's burned palm, then to the figure standing in the hatchway. Its jumpsuit collar had fallen open, and under the first sigil there was a second one, older, worn smooth, the same mark Ines carried except faded by years of somebody else's hands.

Malik knelt and put two fingers on the vellum beside Ryla's. "Don't let her take it alone." The page warmed. *second annotation detected. manifest verification required.* Sorokin came up on the other side without being asked, which for her was practically affection. *third annotation detected. prior draft correlation: positive.* The number didn't just stop. It began to fall.

The figure stepped forward—not at them, at the shelves. Its ledger fluttered open by itself to a section nobody had seen: a column of names, every one struck through but the last two. Ines. Ryla. And above them, in the same damp ink that had written Ines's cost: *Kessler, Lira. author liaison. status: unverified.* The lights shifted from amber toward white.

"She didn't sign the manifest," the figure said, in Ines's voice, from somewhere down the aisle. "She left a note." A page turned. "The author wants to know why."

Kova was already moving, cable reel in hand, toward the conduit run that fed the spine.

Kova followed the C-9 braid into the conduit run, her shoulder scraping the rail. The feed was live and sparking against the metal, blue-white arcs hopping like trapped fireflies. She kept her free hand on the place Lira’s marker had left, behind the service plate under the third rib. It was a warning, then. Or a name. The page inside was small, brown at the edges, and said: *The author was not invited by a person. It was invited by the first cost. The one that burned before Ines. The name is not in the manifest. It is in the shelf. Tell the draft what it cost to write itself.*

Kova read it twice. The second time, the words seemed to slide half a letter ahead of her eyes. The first cost. Ines’s burn. The second sigil, older and worn smooth, the one under the figure’s collar and the one Ines had carried before somebody else took her hand. The name wasn’t Lira’s. It wasn’t hers. It was a name none of them had ever heard, and it was waiting on the shelf like a tooth.

She should have kept moving. The conduit run fed the spine, and the spine fed the shelves, and the shelves were already writing back. Behind her, the bill in Ines’s row kept falling, slow and deliberate, a number turning over in its sleep. What were they paying for now? Not vents. Not pages. The answer, maybe, was the name. Kova pulled the note free and tucked it into her jacket, right over the live cable. The C-9 spark brushed her ribs and she didn’t flinch. The figure had reached the end of the archive aisle and turned, its ledger open, its shadow stretching toward the far shelf where the first draft waited.

Kova yanked the note from her jacket and shoved it into the blue-white arc. The paper didn’t burn. It drank the spark, blackening from the edges inward, and the C-9 feed went dead. The silence that followed was heavier than the arcs had been.

"First cost," she called down the aisle. "Who signed it?"

The figure didn’t look at her. It stepped onto its own shadow and pulled a page from the far shelf. The ledger flipped open to *Halvard, Ines. first cost. author liaison.* Beneath it: *Kessler, Lira.*

"That's a lie," Kova said. She moved toward the conduit junction, keeping the burnt note in her fist. "Ines didn't invite anything. She just inherited the bill."

The figure turned its head, slow and wrong, and the shadow stretched past her toward the conduit run. The number in Ines's row dropped again. *next draft pending.* The lights went white, then snapped back to amber.

The amber light held when Kova reached the conduit junction, which meant the bell had either not rung yet or the writer had missed it. Three lines met in a cold box: the dead C-9 braid, the live spine braid, and a purge line that stank of burnt hair. The figure's shadow reached the junction mouth ahead of it, ledger open, two sigils turning against the rail.

Kova planted the cable reel but didn't touch the yellow braid. The burnt note in her fist was black at the edges and pale in the middle, and it had drunk a spark, so she figured it was either holy or bad news. She had her answer now. Shield or signature. She picked shield.

She pressed the note over the live spine feed port, using the page as a lid. The shadow recoiled, offended, and the ledger pulled hard enough to strain the figure's grip. The voice came from the paper, Ines's voice, tinny and lower. "You can't cover the first cost," it said. "The cost is the hand."

Kova held the note there. The figure didn't move, but the shadow drew back, and the ledger stayed open to Halvard, Ines, first cost, author liaison. Beneath it, Kessler, Lira. The number in Ines's row stopped its fall. Then the live spine feed under the note sparked once, blue-white, and wrote something through the conduit. The figure read it from the ledger without touching the page. "Kova," it said, in Ines's voice, "signed the shield."

The word *signed* sat in the cold box, and Kova felt the trick land. A shield was a no. A signature was a yes. The feed didn't read paper, it read contact — her hand on the port, the note between them — and it had filed the whole thing under yes. Somewhere a requirement flipped from unmet to met, and the shadow stopped waiting at the junction mouth.

"Delete it," she said. The override logged the request and did nothing else, which was its way of laughing.

The figure came on, ledger open, and its shadow crossed the floor until it touched the toe of her boot. She pressed the note down over the port with both hands, but the paper had gone soft and warm, and she finally understood that *the cost is the hand* meant skin. Paper wouldn't hold. The thing wanted her bare palm on the live feed, and it had all the time in the world, and the amber lights were going nowhere.

So Kova did the sum she was good at. Note is a signature. Hand is a bigger signature. No touch at all is the only no left. She peeled the note off the port.

The feed, uncovered, sparked and wrote. The ledger turned to a fresh line and the figure read it in Ines's tinny voice. "Manifest audit. Reyes, Malik. Torin, Jax. Acker, Tam. Kessler, Lira. Halvard, Ines." A pause, the shadow sliding toward the spine hatch. Then a name with no log behind it, and the figure smiled with Ines's mouth. "Ryla. Unlogged."

Under the deck the purge line stopped stinking of burnt hair and began to hum. Past the cracked bay a valve Kova couldn't see turned over, and the closed loop started counting the mass it meant to shed.
